awd_titl_txt: CAREER: Transnational Lives in the U.S.
awd_abstract_narration:
The project uses the experiences of a group in movement to examine that movement along three main lines of inquiry.  First, the project investigates the motivations for movement: what factors motivate a larger grouping and this group in particular, to leave their home region to come to a new home? Second, it examines the process: How do home region ideals and destination region policies affect the movement process? Third, it investigates the consequences of movement: How does movement shape the life of those who have moved and the life of family and close relatives left behind?  This project situates these experiences in the transnationalism theoretical framework to explore the global processes and conditions that are significantly shaping the lines of citizenship, culture, economic development, and the structure of society.  

The three lines of inquiry will be addressed with three different methods: using an archive of 2000 letters, oral histories of 100 families with two interviews per family, and ethnographic data collected over 14 months from three relevant communities.  Coding of these data will be organized according to eight domains: education, economics, identity, housing, intimate life, health, and other important social domains. Students will assist in this research after being trained to conduct research across cultures.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project studied Ghanaian migration to the United States by asking three basic questions: why people leave, how they move through the migration process, and what happens after migration for migrants and the families they remain connected to. The project began from the idea that migration is not only a search for opportunity. It is also a response to disappointment, blocked futures, and the failures of states to provide enough security, dignity, or possibility for their citizens.

Over the life of the award, I conducted approximately fourteen months of fieldwork in Accra, Ghana; Houston, Texas; and the Bronx, New York. In Ghana, I spent time with people who aspired to migrate, people preparing applications, people who had been denied visas, and families with relatives abroad. In the United States, I spent time with Ghanaian migrants in restaurants, churches, homes, football fields, and community spaces. These everyday sites made it possible to study migration not only as a legal or economic process, but as a lived social world shaped by work, documentation, family obligation, faith, friendship, fear, humor, and hope.

The project also included nearly forty interviews with Ghanaian migrants in the United States and about forty interviews with Ghanaians in Ghana who either hoped to migrate or had family members abroad. These interviews helped show migration from both sides of the journey: the desire to leave and the reality of life after arrival. The research shows that Ghana never disappears from migrants’ lives. Migrants continue to send money home, follow Ghanaian politics, support relatives, respond to family crises, and imagine return. At the same time, life in the United States does not always resolve the problems that migration was meant to solve. Legal status, work, family separation, and the feeling of not fully belonging remain central challenges.

During the award period, the project also expanded methodologically. In addition to ethnography and interviews, I developed a visual archive of nearly 2,000 photographs of about 500 Ghanaians in Ghana and the United States. I also created a historical archive of migration-related discussions in major Ghanaian newspapers and began work with a family archive of letters. Together, these materials allow the project to tell a fuller story of migration across time: in public debate, in private family correspondence, in oral histories, in photographs, and in everyday life.

The intellectual merit of the project lies in its contribution to the study of migration, race, citizenship, and the nation-state. The project argues that migration should be understood not only as movement across borders, but also as a critique of the conditions that make leaving feel necessary. For Black migrants in particular, the research shows how people often move between two unequal political orders: one state that failed to provide enough possibility and another that does not always fully protect or include them.

The broader impacts of the project include student training, public education, and the preservation of migrant stories. The project trained students in qualitative research methods, including interviewing, archival work, transcription, coding, and the use of NVivo. It also generated materials that can be used in future teaching, public talks, exhibits, and community-facing projects. Although no publications have yet come out of the award because the grant period was devoted to data collection, the project has created the foundation for a major book and related articles. More broadly, it offers a more human and grounded account of migration—one that shows migrants not only as workers, visa applicants, or remittance senders, but as full people building lives across borders.
